branch_provenance.syndrome: Subacute Multisystem Syndrome with Generalized Vesicles and Bullae, Hepatobiliary Involvement, and Eosinophilia

state.case_summary:
A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Toxic epidermal necrolysis
B. The eruption began shortly after ciprofloxacin exposure
C. The extent of skin and mucosal involvement meets criteria for TEN rather than milder reactions
D. Histopathology confirms epidermal necrolysis rather than other bullous diseases
E. Biopsy and clinical features rule out mimics such as SSSS, pemphigus/pemphigoid, AGEP, and GVHD
F. Obstructive biliary pathology is excluded as a cause of jaundice
G. Necrotizing fasciitis is unlikely given absence of severe localized pain, crepitus, edema, necrosis, or malodorous
H. None

excluded_candidates: Infection: although surgical-site infection and persistent fever are noted, the presence of eosinophilia and the pattern of skin and liver involvement suggest other mechanisms may be at play
Autoimmune hepatitis: although liver enzyme elevations are significant, the context of recent antibiotic use and eosinophilia suggests a possible drug-induced or allergic component
Primary biliary cirrhosis: less likely given the acute onset and presence of skin lesions
